source: Depreciation curves follow the shape every major used-car guide publishes: steepest in year one, flattening after year five. The ownership-cost shares follow the AAA 'Your Driving Costs' breakdown. The 20/3/8 guidance is a lender-and-counsellor convention, not a law.
confidenceNote: Every figure here is a shape, not a prediction about a particular car. Depreciation depends on the model, the mileage and the year you sell; insurance depends on you. Treat the totals as an order of magnitude — the point is that the sticker price is not the cost.
note: `retainedShare` is the fraction of the purchase price a typical car is still worth after that many years. The gap between two rows is the depreciation you paid to own it over that stretch.

depreciation.note: The steepest year by far. Buying at one year old is the single biggest lever on the whole page.
Roughly half. The curve is much flatter from here.

runningCosts.label: Insurance
runningCosts.note: Varies more by driver and postcode than by car.

runningCosts.label: Fuel or charging
runningCosts.note: The one most people think of first, and it is under a quarter.

runningCosts.label: Maintenance and tyres
runningCosts.note: Low and predictable early, then not.

runningCosts.label: Interest on the loan
runningCosts.note: Zero if you did not borrow. This is the part a longer term inflates.

loanGuidance.what: Put 20% down, borrow for no more than three years, and keep the payment under 8% of what you earn in a month before tax.
loanGuidance.why: It is not a rule about cars. It is a test of whether the car fits the life: if you cannot pass it, the car is more expensive than the household can carry, whatever the monthly figure says.
loanGuidance.note: Seven- and eight-year loans are now ordinary. They pass no version of this test — they make the monthly figure small by keeping you in debt past the point the car is worth what you owe.

underwater.what: Owing more than the car is worth
underwater.why: Depreciation is fastest in year one and a long loan pays the principal down slowly, so the two curves cross late. Until they do you cannot sell without writing a cheque, and an insurer paying out a write-off pays the car's value, not your balance.
underwater.note: This is the concrete harm of a long term, and it is the one a monthly payment hides completely.

leaseVsBuy.label: Leasing
leaseVsBuy.suits: A short, known period; a fixed monthly cost; no interest in what it is worth at the end.
leaseVsBuy.costs: You pay the steepest part of the depreciation curve and own nothing at the end of it. Mileage caps and wear charges are real money.

leaseVsBuy.label: Buying new
leaseVsBuy.suits: Keeping a car a long time — past year seven the early depreciation stops mattering much.
leaseVsBuy.costs: You buy the whole first-year drop, which is the most expensive year a car ever has.

leaseVsBuy.label: Buying at one to three years old
leaseVsBuy.costs: Someone else has taken the first-year hit. You take a shorter warranty and an unknown history, which an inspection is for.
